html:
Bhutan is a small Buddhist kingdom in the eastern Himalayas, between Tibet and India. The map shows it from 1200 to 2010. Before 1600 its valleys were held by local lords and Buddhist lineages tied to Tibet. Legend says the teacher Padmasambhava brought Buddhism there in the 700s.

The state was made by Ngawang Namgyal, a lama of the Drukpa school who fled Tibet in 1616 (Zhabdrung unifies Bhutan). He beat back Tibetan invasions, built dzongs, the fortress monasteries that still serve as seats of government, and set up a dual system with a religious head and a civil ruler. The country's own name, Druk Yul, means land of the thunder dragon, after his school.

Later turning points:

  • In the Duar War of 1864 and 1865 Britain took the strip of plains along its southern border.
  • In 1907 the leading lords chose Ugyen Wangchuck as hereditary king. His family still reigns.
  • Britain, and from 1949 India, guided its foreign affairs, while it stayed closed to most visitors.
  • In the 1970s the fourth king spoke of Gross National Happiness as the country's goal.
  • In the early 1990s around 100,000 Nepali speaking southerners left or were forced out (Bhutanese refugees).

In 2008 Bhutan became a constitutional monarchy and held its first national elections.
